title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: The Daixin Team is a ransomware and data extortion group that has targeted U.S. businesses, predominantly in the Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) Sector, since at least June 2022. It encrypted servers supporting healthcare services including electronic health records (EHR), diagnostics, imaging and intranet systems, and stole personally identifiable information (PII) and patient health information (PHI). Third-party reporting says its ransomware is based on leaked Babuk Locker source code.

title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: Daixin actors gain access through virtual private network (VPN) servers. In one confirmed case they likely exploited an unpatched VPN server vulnerability (T1190). In another they used previously compromised credentials to access a legacy VPN server without MFA (T1078 Valid Accounts). VPN credentials were likely obtained via a phishing email with a malicious attachment (T1598.002 Spearphishing Attachment).

title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: Actors moved laterally with RDP (T1563.002 RDP Hijacking) and SSH (T1563.001 SSH Hijacking). They attempted to obtain privileged credentials through credential dumping (T1003) and pass the hash (T1550.002). Privileged accounts were used to reset passwords for VMware ESXi servers (T1098 Account Manipulation) through VMware vCenter Server, and SSH was used to connect to ESXi servers for ransomware deployment.

title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: Daixin used Rclone to exfiltrate data to a dedicated virtual private server, and Ngrok as a reverse proxy for exfiltration (T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service). Stolen PII and PHI were used to threaten release if the ransom was not paid.

title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: The ransomware encrypts ESXi-hosted files and specific VM-related file extensions, disrupting healthcare services (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact).

title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team
text: Promptly patch VPNs, remote access and virtualization software, prioritizing known exploited vulnerabilities. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on webmail, VPNs, critical systems and privileged and backup accounts. Restrict, monitor and log RDP; require MFA, use VPN or VDI for external access and disable unused ports such as 3389. Disable unneeded ports, protocols and external management interfaces (SSH, Telnet, HTTP). Segment networks into tiers for critical systems. Use PKI and certificates to authenticate connections to networks, IoT medical devices and EHR systems. Apply least privilege. Encrypt PII/PHI at rest and in transit, store patient data only on protected internal systems, and follow HIPAA security practices. Monitor IoT medical devices for erratic behavior. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups, test restoration, and maintain an incident response and breach notification plan. Limit SMB and remove SMBv1.

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: LockBit 3.0, also known as "LockBit Black", is a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) variant and a continuation of LockBit 2.0 and LockBit. The advisory notes code similarities with BlackMatter and BlackCat ransomware. Affiliates deploy it against a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure organizations. Before encrypting data, affiliates steal files and threaten to publish them on Tor darknet leak sites. The FBI, CISA and MS-ISAC recommend hardening credentials, phishing-resistant MFA, patching, network segmentation and immutable offline backups.

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: LockBit 3.0 affiliates gain initial access through exploitation of Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and other external remote services (T1133), drive-by compromise (T1189), phishing and spearphishing campaigns (T1566), abuse of valid accounts (T1078), and exploitation of public-facing applications (T1190).

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: Affiliates used the Chocolatey package manager as a software deployment tool (T1072). The malware can enable automatic logon to persist and escalate privileges (T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution). LockBit 3.0 sends encrypted host and bot information to its C2 servers (T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information), deletes itself from disk after running (T1070.004 File Deletion), and requires a password to decrypt and launch its main component (T1480.001 Execution Guardrails: Environmental Keying), which hinders analysis.

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
section: Credential Access, Discovery and Lateral Movement
text: Affiliates dumped LSASS memory with ProcDump (T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory). They scanned networks with SoftPerfect Network Scanner (T1046 Network Service Discovery) and enumerated hostnames, domains, drives and shares (T1082 System Information Discovery). The malware skips systems whose language settings match an exclusion list (T1614.001 System Language Discovery). Splashtop remote desktop software was used for lateral movement (T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol). FileZilla was used for C2 (T1071.002 File Transfer Protocols) and Plink to automate SSH actions (T1572 Protocol Tunnel).

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: Custom: Stealbit (exfiltration) and the LockBit 3.0 encryptor. Freeware and open-source tools repurposed by affiliates: rclone, MEGA MegaSync, Impacket, Sysinternals PsExec and ProcDump, Mimikatz, Ngrok, Plink, FileZilla, WinSCP, Splashtop, SoftPerfect Network Scanner and Chocolatey. Penetration-testing frameworks Metasploit and Cobalt Strike were also observed, and PowerShell and batch scripts were seen in most intrusions.

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: Before encryption, affiliates exfiltrate sensitive files using Stealbit, rclone (T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage), MEGA and public file-sharing services (T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service). The ransom note threatens to publish data on Tor leak sites and warns that competitors could buy it.

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: LockBit 3.0 encrypts data on local and remote devices (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact), terminates processes and services (T1489 Service Stop), deletes volume shadow copies (T1490 Inhibit System Recovery), deletes logs and empties the recycle bin (T1485 Data Destruction), and changes the wallpaper and icons to LockBit branding (T1491.001 Internal Defacement).

title: #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0
text: Keep multiple copies of sensitive data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, secure location. Apply NIST password guidance (long passwords, hashing, no reuse, lockout after failed attempts). Require phishing-resistant MFA for webmail, VPNs and critical systems. Keep operating systems, software and firmware patched. Segment networks to limit lateral movement. Log and monitor network traffic and use EDR to detect lateral connections. Keep antivirus updated with real-time detection on all hosts. Audit domain controllers, servers, workstations and Active Directory for new or unrecognized accounts. Enforce least privilege and just-in-time administrative access. Disable unused ports. Add external-sender email banners and disable hyperlinks in received email. Disable command-line and scripting activity where possible. Maintain encrypted, immutable, offline backups covering the whole organization and test restoration. Validate security controls against the advisory's ATT&CK techniques.

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Rhysida ransomware has been observed since May 2023 targeting education, healthcare, manufacturing, information technology and government organizations as "targets of opportunity". Open-source reporting notes similarities with Vice Society (DEV-0832) activity and indicates Rhysida operates as Ransomware-as-a-Service, with ransoms split between the group and affiliates.

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Rhysida actors abuse valid credentials on VPN access points, often where MFA was not enabled (T1078 Valid Accounts). They exploited Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) in Microsoft Netlogon (T1190) and conducted successful phishing attacks (T1566).

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Actors ran PowerShell discovery commands and scripts (T1059.001), often in hidden windows (T1564.003), and batch scripts via cmd.exe to stage the ransomware (T1059.003). The encryptor PE is injected into running processes (T1055.002 Portable Executable Injection). They cleared System, Application and Security logs with wevtutil (T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs), deleted the encryptor after running (T1070.004) and modified the registry via cmd.exe (T1112).

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Actors dumped NTDS credentials with secretsdump and ntdsutil (T1003.003 NTDS). Discovery used ipconfig (T1016), net group (T1018, T1069.002), whoami and net (T1033), net localgroup (T1069.001), net user (T1087.002) and nltest for domain trusts (T1482). PowerView was used for reconnaissance.

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Lateral movement used RDP (T1021.001), PuTTY over SSH (T1021.004) and heavy use of PsExec. AnyDesk was used for remote access and persistence (T1219). PortStarter, a Go-based backdoor, modifies firewall settings and opens ports to C2 servers. The encryptor has been seen named conhost.exe.

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Rhysida encrypts data using a 4096-bit RSA key with ChaCha20 (T1486). It practices double extortion, threatening to publish exfiltrated data, with Bitcoin payment (T1657). A PDF ransom note named "CriticalBreachDetected" provides a unique code and a Tor portal.

title: #StopRansomware: Rhysida Ransomware
text: Prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems. Require phishing-resistant MFA for webmail, VPNs and critical-system accounts. Restrict command-line and scripting use; restrict PowerShell via Group Policy to specific administrators and upgrade it. Enable command-line auditing, process tracking and enhanced PowerShell logging with at least 180 days retention, forwarded to a hardened central log server. Limit RDP to known users with MFA and Remote Credential Guard, log attempts and enforce lockouts. Allowlist approved remote access tools. Segment networks, monitor with EDR, apply least privilege and just-in-time access. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups in a separate location and test them. Add external email banners and disable hyperlinks.

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
text: The Play ransomware group (also known as Playcrypt) has affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America and Europe since June 2022, with incidents in Australia from April to November 2023. The FBI was aware of about 300 affected entities as of October 2023. Play is presumed to be a closed group designed to "guarantee the secrecy of deals" rather than a RaaS.

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
text: Play actors abuse valid accounts (T1078) and exploit public-facing applications (T1190), specifically FortiOS vulnerabilities CVE-2018-13379 and CVE-2020-12812 and Microsoft Exchange ProxyNotShell (CVE-2022-41040, CVE-2022-41082). They also use external-facing services such as RDP and VPN (T1133 External Remote Services).

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
text: Play uses AdFind for Active Directory queries and Grixba to enumerate network configuration and scan for antivirus (T1016, T1518.001 Security Software Discovery). GMER, IOBit and PowerTool are used to disable antivirus and remove log files (T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools, T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs).

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
section: Credential Access, Lateral Movement and C2
text: Actors search for unsecured credentials (T1552) and use Mimikatz to dump credentials (T1003), plus WinPEAS to find privilege escalation paths. C2 and lateral movement use Cobalt Strike, SystemBC and PsExec. Executables are distributed within the environment (T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer) and through Group Policy Objects (T1484.001 Group Policy Modification).

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
text: Play splits and compresses data into .RAR files with WinRAR (T1560.001) and moves them with WinSCP to actor-controlled accounts (T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol). Encryption uses AES-RSA hybrid with intermittent encryption, skipping system files; encrypted files get a .play extension and a ReadMe.txt note is placed in C:\ (T1486). Double extortion: the note has no initial demand and directs victims to an email address; payment in cryptocurrency; refusal leads to publication on a Tor leak site (T1657).

title: #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware
text: Keep multiple copies of sensitive data in segmented, secure locations. Follow NIST password guidance. Require administrator credentials to install software. Require MFA for webmail, VPN and critical systems. Prioritize patching of known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems; deploy the latest Exchange updates or disable OWA if patching is not possible. Segment networks, monitor traffic including lateral movement, and use EDR. Filter traffic from unknown origins to internal remote services. Audit accounts and AD, apply least privilege and just-in-time admin access. Disable unused ports and scripting where possible. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups and test restoration.

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: ALPHV Blackcat is a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) operation whose administrators provide the platform to affiliates. A rewritten variant, "ALPHV Blackcat Ransomware 2.0 Sphynx", announced in February 2023, can encrypt Windows and Linux devices and VMware instances. The healthcare sector was the most commonly victimized sector since mid-December 2023, out of nearly 70 leaked victims. Some affiliates steal data and extort victims without deploying ransomware at all.

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: Affiliates use social engineering: they pose as company IT or helpdesk staff by phone call or SMS to obtain employee credentials (T1598 Phishing for Information), using open-source research on the target. They use compromised accounts to gain access (T1586 Compromise Accounts), and adversary-in-the-middle phishing with Evilginx2 to capture MFA codes, login credentials and session cookies (T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle).

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: Affiliates obtained passwords from local networks, deleted servers and domain controllers to move laterally (T1555 Credentials from Password Stores). They used Kerberos token generation for domain access, including creating an account named "aadmin" (T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets).

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: Remote access: AnyDesk, Mega sync, Splashtop; also SimpleHelp, ScreenConnect and MeshCentral in IOC tables. Tunneling: Plink and Ngrok. C2 beacons: Brute Ratel C4 and Cobalt Strike. Credential capture: Evilginx2. Metasploit was abused as an allowlisted application for defense evasion. POORTRY and STONESTOP were used to terminate security processes (T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools).

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: Data is exfiltrated with Mega.nz or Dropbox (T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage). After exfiltration and/or encryption (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact), actors contact victims through Tor, Tox, email or encrypted apps. Affiliates offer paid "vulnerability reports" and "security recommendations". The ransom note follows the pattern RECOVER-(seven-digit extension) FILES.txt.

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: Regularly inventory authorized and unauthorized devices and software. Prioritize remediation of known exploited vulnerabilities. Enforce MFA with strong passwords, preferably phishing-resistant FIDO/WebAuthn or PKI-based MFA, because Blackcat affiliates bypass weaker MFA with adversary-in-the-middle phishing. Close unused ports and remove unnecessary applications. Use application allowlisting and block portable or unauthorized remote access programs; secure approved remote access tools per CISA guidance. Monitor network traffic including lateral movement, use EDR, monitor internal email and messaging and establish a traffic baseline. Train users to recognize and report helpdesk-impersonation social engineering and phishing. Validate controls against the listed ATT&CK techniques.

title: #StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat
text: If compromise is detected: isolate affected hosts, reimage compromised systems, issue new account credentials, collect and review artifacts such as running processes, network connections and logs, and report the incident to CISA and the FBI (IC3).

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Akira ransomware has been active since March 2023 and has impacted a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure entities in North America, Europe and Australia. Variants include the original C++ Windows encryptor (appends .akira), the Rust-based Megazord (appends .powerranges), and Akira_v2, a Rust-based encryptor for VMware ESXi and Linux. Akira uses double extortion: it exfiltrates data before encrypting systems.

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Akira actors mainly gain access through VPN services without multifactor authentication, largely by exploiting Cisco vulnerabilities CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). Other vectors are external-facing services such as RDP (T1133 External Remote Services), spearphishing attachments and links (T1566.001, T1566.002), and abuse of valid credentials (T1078).

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Actors created new domain accounts, for example "itadm", for persistence (T1136.002 Create Account: Domain Account). They dumped credentials with Mimikatz and LaZagne (T1003 OS Credential Dumping) including LSASS memory access (T1003.001). Veeam credential tools (VeeamHax, Veeam-GetCreds.ps1) and Kerberos ticket dumping were also observed.

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Discovery used SoftPerfect and Advanced IP Scanner (T1016), nltest /dclist (T1018 Remote System Discovery), nltest and net for domain trusts (T1482), PCHunter64 (T1082), tasklist (T1057) and net group/localgroup commands (T1069). To disable antivirus, actors used a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) approach with PowerTool and the Zemana AntiMalware driver (T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools).

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Remote access and C2 used AnyDesk, MobaXterm, RustDesk (T1219 Remote Access Software), Ngrok and Cloudflare Tunnel (T1090 Proxy). Data was compressed and split with WinRAR (T1560.001), then exfiltrated with WinSCP and FileZilla (T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol), CloudZilla (T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account) and RClone to cloud storage such as Mega (T1567.002).

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Akira encrypts systems with a hybrid ChaCha20/RSA scheme (T1486) and deletes volume shadow copies (T1490 Inhibit System Recovery). No initial ransom demand is left; each victim gets a unique code and a .onion URL. Payment is demanded in Bitcoin, and actors threaten to publish data on Tor and have called victim companies (T1657 Financial Theft).

title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware
text: Keep multiple copies of sensitive data in a physically separate, secure location. Require long NIST-compliant passwords. Enable MFA for all services, especially webmail, VPNs and critical systems — VPNs without MFA were the main entry point. Patch internet-facing systems, prioritizing known exploited vulnerabilities such as the Cisco ASA/FTD flaws. Segment networks, monitor traffic and use EDR. Block unknown or untrusted origins from reaching remote access services. Audit Active Directory for new or unrecognized accounts. Apply least privilege and just-in-time admin access. Disable unused ports and command-line/scripting where possible. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups and test restoration.

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Black Basta is a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) variant first identified in April 2022. As of May 2024 its affiliates had impacted over 500 organizations globally, mainly in North America, Europe and Australia, encrypting and stealing data from at least 12 of 16 critical infrastructure sectors, including Healthcare and Public Health (HPH).

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Affiliates primarily use spearphishing (T1566). Researchers also reported Qakbot as an initial access vector. Starting February 2024, affiliates exploited ConnectWise ScreenConnect vulnerability CVE-2024-1709 (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). Valid credentials were abused in some cases (T1078). A newer social-engineering pattern combines email bombing with phone calls or Microsoft Teams messages in which the actor poses as technical support (T1566.004 Spearphishing Voice) and convinces users to install remote access tools such as Quick Assist or AnyDesk (T1204 User Execution).

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
section: Discovery, Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion
text: Affiliates used SoftPerfect network scanner (netscan.exe) for discovery, and ran reconnaissance tools with innocuous file names such as "Intel" or "Dell" (T1036 Masquerading). For privilege escalation they used credential scraping with Mimikatz and exploited ZeroLogon, NoPac and PrintNightmare (T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation). A tool called Backstab was used to disable EDR (T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools), and PowerShell was used to disable antivirus products (T1059.001).

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Lateral movement used BITSAdmin, PsExec, Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), Splashtop, ScreenConnect and Cobalt Strike beacons. Remote access tools include AnyDesk, Microsoft Quick Assist, ScreenConnect and Splashtop.

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Black Basta uses double extortion. Data is exfiltrated with RClone and in some cases WinSCP to actor-controlled accounts. Ransom notes usually omit a ransom demand or payment instructions and instead provide a unique code and a Tor .onion URL. Victims typically have 10 to 12 days to pay before data is published on the "Basta News" leak site.

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Affiliates delete volume shadow copies with vssadmin.exe (T1490 Inhibit System Recovery) and encrypt files using ChaCha20 with an RSA-4096 public key (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact).

title: #StopRansomware: Black Basta
text: Install OS, software and firmware updates promptly, prioritizing Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV). Require phishing-resistant MFA, especially for privileged accounts. Train users to recognize and report phishing and help-desk impersonation. Secure remote access software following joint guidance. Back up critical systems and device configurations. Apply the #StopRansomware Guide. HPH organizations should know all assets and dependencies, protect ePHI, and prioritize vulnerability management using KEV, EPSS, CVSS and SSVC. Validate security controls against the advisory's ATT&CK techniques.

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
text: Ghost actors, located in China, have conducted financially motivated ransomware attacks since early 2021 against organizations in more than 70 countries, including critical infrastructure, schools and universities, healthcare, government networks, religious institutions, technology and manufacturing companies, and small and medium-sized businesses. The group rotates names and file extensions; aliases include Cring, Crypt3r, Phantom, Strike, Hello, Wickrme, HsHarada and Rapture. Samples include Cring.exe, Ghost.exe, ElysiumO.exe and Locker.exe.

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
text: Ghost gains access by exploiting public-facing applications with known, unpatched CVEs (T1190): Fortinet FortiOS CVE-2018-13379, Adobe ColdFusion CVE-2010-2861 and CVE-2009-3960, Microsoft SharePoint CVE-2019-0604, and the Microsoft Exchange ProxyShell chain (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207). Web shells are uploaded for persistence (T1505.003).

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
text: Actors use PowerShell to deploy Cobalt Strike Beacon (T1059.001), cmd.exe to download content (T1059.003) and WMI to run PowerShell on other systems (T1047). Privilege escalation uses open-source tools such as BadPotato, GodPotato, SharpZeroLogon and SharpGPPPass (T1068) and SYSTEM token theft (T1134.001). Actors change passwords of existing accounts (T1098) and create local and domain accounts (T1136.001, T1136.002).

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
section: Defense Evasion, Credential Access and Discovery
text: Ghost disables antivirus including Windows Defender (T1562.001), hides PowerShell activity (T1564.003) and clears Windows event logs (T1070.001). Credentials are dumped with hashdump and Mimikatz (T1003). Discovery uses Ladon 911 and SharpNBTScan (T1018), process listing (T1057), domain admin enumeration (T1087.002), SharpShares (T1135) and security software discovery (T1518.001).

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
section: Command and Control, Exfiltration and Impact
text: C2 runs over HTTP/HTTPS via Cobalt Strike (T1071.001); IOX is used as a reverse proxy. Exfiltration is limited — usually less than hundreds of gigabytes — via the C2 channel and web shells (T1041) and limited Mega.nz use (T1567.002). Ghost actors typically spend only a short time in a network before deploying ransomware. It encrypts files (T1486), disables the Volume Shadow Copy Service and deletes shadow copies (T1490). Demands are typically tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in cryptocurrency; notes claim stolen data will be sold.

title: #StopRansomware: Ghost (Cring) Ransomware
text: Keep known-good backups offline or segmented from source systems. Patch operating systems, software and firmware promptly, especially the exploited Fortinet, ColdFusion, SharePoint and Exchange flaws. Segment networks. Require phishing-resistant MFA for privileged and email accounts. Train users on phishing. Monitor for unauthorized PowerShell use and apply least privilege. Allowlist applications, scripts and network traffic. Alert on unusual network activity such as scans, admin account changes and unexpected scripts. Disable unused ports such as RDP, FTP 21 and SMB 445 or restrict them behind VPN/firewalls. Use email filtering with DMARC, DKIM and SPF.

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Medusa is a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) variant first identified in June 2021. It began as a closed operation and later moved to an affiliate model, though developers still control ransom negotiation. As of February 2025, over 300 victims were affected across medical, education, legal, insurance, technology and manufacturing sectors. Medusa is unrelated to MedusaLocker and to the Medusa mobile malware.

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Medusa developers recruit initial access brokers (IABs) on cybercriminal forums. Access is also gained through phishing to steal credentials (T1566) and exploitation of unpatched vulnerabilities (T1190) including ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709 and Fortinet EMS SQL injection CVE-2023-48788.

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Medusa actors rely on living-off-the-land tools. They delete previously installed tools and PowerShell command history (T1070, T1070.003), obfuscate strings and run base64-encoded commands (T1027, T1027.013), and attempt to kill or delete EDR tools, sometimes using vulnerable or signed drivers (T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools).

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Network enumeration used Advanced IP Scanner and SoftPerfect Network Scanner (T1046). Actors enumerated files (T1083), shares (T1135), network configuration (T1016), system information via systeminfo (T1082) and domain groups (T1069.002). Mimikatz was used to dump LSASS (T1003.001).

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
section: Lateral Movement and Command and Control
text: Lateral movement used RDP (T1021.001), PsExec to run payloads as SYSTEM (T1569.002), PowerShell and cmd.exe (T1059.001, T1059.003), WMI (T1047), and many legitimate remote access tools (T1219): AnyDesk, Atera, ConnectWise, eHorus, N-able, SimpleHelp and Splashtop. PDQ Deploy and BigFix were used to deploy the encryptor (T1072 Software Deployment Tools). Tools were transferred with PowerShell, cmd and certutil (T1105). A powerfun.ps1 stager created TLS reverse or bind shells over port 443 (T1071.001), and Ligolo and Cloudflared were used for tunneling. A domain account was created for persistence (T1136.002).

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Rclone sends data to Medusa C2 servers (T1567.002). The encryptor gaze.exe encrypts files with AES-256 and the .medusa extension (T1486), deletes shadow copies (T1490), stops backup, security and database services (T1489) and manually shuts down and encrypts virtual machines (T1529). Medusa uses double extortion with a .onion leak site and countdown timers; victims can pay $10,000 to add a day. The note gives 48 hours to make contact via Tor chat or Tox. One victim was contacted by a second actor after paying, a possible triple-extortion scheme.

title: #StopRansomware: Medusa Ransomware
text: Keep multiple copies of sensitive data and servers in separate secure locations. Follow NIST password standards. Require MFA for webmail, VPNs and critical systems. Patch, prioritizing known exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems. Segment networks, monitor traffic with EDR, and require VPNs or jump hosts for remote access. Monitor for unauthorized scanning and block unknown origins from internal remote services. Audit admin accounts, apply least privilege and check AD for unrecognized accounts. Disable unnecessary command-line and scripting and unused ports. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups and test restoration.

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: Interlock is a financially motivated, opportunistic ransomware operation first observed in late September 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure in North America and Europe. Open-source reporting notes similarities with Rhysida ransomware. Interlock has encryptors for Windows, Linux and FreeBSD, and encrypted files use the .1nt3rlock extension.

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: Unusually for ransomware, Interlock gains access through drive-by downloads from compromised legitimate websites (T1189 Drive-by Compromise), using fake Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge updates and later files masquerading as security software updates. It also uses the "ClickFix" technique: fake CAPTCHA pages that trick users into pasting and running a Base64-encoded PowerShell command (T1204.004 Malicious Copy and Paste).

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: PowerShell scripts drop files, change the registry and perform reconnaissance (T1059.001). Persistence uses a Startup folder file and a "Chrome Updater" Run key (T1547.001, T1036.005 Masquerading). Discovery commands include WindowsIdentity.GetCurrent() (T1033), systeminfo and Get-PSDrive (T1082), tasklist /svc and Get-Service (T1007) and arp -a (T1016).

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: Interlock runs Lumma Stealer and Berserk Stealer (T1056 Input Capture), a keylogger klg.dll that logs to conhost.txt (T1056.001) and cht.exe to steal browser credentials (T1555.003). Kerberoasting may have been used to compromise domain admin accounts (T1558.003). Valid and domain accounts are reused for lateral movement (T1078, T1078.002) over RDP (T1021.001), with AnyDesk, PuTTY, PsExec and ScreenConnect (T1219). Cobalt Strike, SystemBC, Interlock RAT and NodeSnake RAT provide C2.

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: Azure Storage Explorer is used to browse victims' Azure storage (T1530), AzCopy uploads data to Azure blob storage (T1567.002) and WinSCP is also used (T1048). After encryption a DLL is run with rundll32 (T1218.011) and deletes the encryption binary (T1070.004). Data is encrypted with AES/RSA (T1486). Double extortion: notes give a unique code and Tor .onion URL with no initial demand, payment is in Bitcoin, and actors have published stolen data on their leak site.

title: #StopRansomware: Interlock
text: Use DNS filtering and web access firewalls to block malicious sites. Train users to spot social engineering such as fake updates and ClickFix fake CAPTCHAs. Keep multiple copies of critical data in separate locations. Use long NIST passwords and require MFA broadly after implementing ICAM. Patch internet-facing systems, prioritizing known exploited vulnerabilities. Deploy EDR on VMs, systems and networks. Segment networks and monitor traffic. Block untrusted origins from internal remote services. Audit AD for unrecognized accounts, enforce least privilege and just-in-time admin. Disable unused ports and command-line/scripting where not required. Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups and test restoration.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text:
1. Determine which systems were impacted and immediately isolate them. If several systems or subnets appear impacted, take the network offline at the switch level. If that is not immediately possible, unplug affected devices or remove them from Wi-Fi. For cloud resources, take a snapshot of volumes for later forensic review.
2. Coordinate isolation using out-of-band communication such as phone calls, because attackers may be monitoring email and chat and could otherwise move laterally or deploy ransomware more widely.
3. Power down devices only as a last resort, if they cannot be disconnected from the network, because shutting down destroys evidence in volatile memory.
4. Triage impacted systems for restoration using a predefined critical asset list (health and safety, revenue, critical services and their dependencies). Track systems that were not impacted so they can be deprioritized.
5. Review antivirus, EDR, IDS/IPS and logs for evidence of earlier "dropper" malware such as Bumblebee, Dridex, Emotet, QakBot or Anchor — ransomware may indicate a previous, unresolved compromise.
6. Confer with the incident response team and document an initial understanding of what happened.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: Enterprise hunting priorities: newly created or escalated Active Directory accounts; suspicious VPN and other logins; misuse of built-in tools that impair recovery such as bcdedit.exe, vssadmin.exe and wbadmin.exe; Cobalt Strike beacons; unexpected remote monitoring and management (RMM) software; unexpected PowerShell or PsTools/PsExec use; credential dumping (Mimikatz, NTDSutil.exe); unusual endpoint-to-endpoint traffic; data exfiltration tools such as Rclone, Rsync and FTP/SFTP; and new services or scheduled tasks. Cloud: enable tools that detect and prevent changes to IAM, network security and data protection resources, and automate responses such as disabling overly permissive firewall rules.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: Follow the incident response and communications plan to notify internal and external stakeholders: IT, managed security providers, cyber insurer, and senior leadership. Consider reporting to CISA, the local FBI field office, the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or the U.S. Secret Service, and request assistance. Coordinate accurate internal and external messaging with communications staff. If data was breached, follow breach notification requirements. CISA, MS-ISAC and federal law enforcement do not recommend paying a ransom: payment does not guarantee decryption and attackers have issued follow-on extortion demands.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: If no initial mitigation is possible, capture system images and memory from a sample of affected devices, collect logs, precursor malware samples and IOCs, prioritizing volatile or short-retention data such as memory, Windows Security logs and firewall buffers. Consult federal law enforcement about possible decryptors. Research trusted guidance for the specific variant; stop or disable known ransomware binaries and remove associated registry values and files. Identify the systems and accounts involved in the initial breach, including email accounts. Based on breach details, contain further access by disabling VPNs, remote access servers, single sign-on resources and public-facing cloud assets as needed.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: If an infected workstation is encrypting server data: review Sessions and Open Files on affected servers; check file ownership and ransom notes for the associated user; review TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager logs for RDP connections; review Windows Security, SMB and related logs; and run a packet capture (for example Wireshark) on the server with a filter to identify IP addresses actively writing or renaming files.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: Investigate outside-in persistence (rogue accounts, perimeter backdoors, exploitable external vulnerabilities) and inside-out persistence (malware implants, living-off-the-land tools such as Cobalt Strike or PsExec, PowerShell scripts) using EDR, account audits, centralized logs and forensics. Rebuild systems by priority of critical services using pre-configured standard images or infrastructure-as-code templates. Once the environment is fully cleaned and rebuilt, reset passwords for all affected systems and accounts, remove malicious persistence, apply patches and upgrades, and rotate customer-managed encryption keys. The designated IT or security authority declares the incident over based on established criteria.

title: CISA Ransomware Response Checklist (#StopRansomware Guide, Part 2)
text: Reconnect systems and restore data from offline, encrypted backups based on critical-service priority. Ensure only clean systems join the recovery network, for example a new VLAN. Document lessons learned and update policies, plans and procedures. Consider sharing lessons learned and IOCs with CISA or the sector ISAC.

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Maintain offline, encrypted, immutable backups that cover the whole organization, stored in a physically separate, segmented location, and regularly test restoration. Ransomware groups routinely delete volume shadow copies (T1490) and target backup software credentials (for example Akira's Veeam credential tools), so online backups and shadow copies alone are not sufficient. Recommended in: LockBit 3.0, Akira, Play, Rhysida, Medusa, Ghost, Daixin, Interlock, Black Basta.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO/WebAuthn or PKI) for webmail, VPNs, remote access and privileged and backup accounts. VPNs without MFA were the main entry point for Akira, Rhysida and Daixin, and ALPHV Blackcat affiliates bypassed weaker MFA using adversary-in-the-middle phishing (Evilginx2). Follow NIST password guidance and audit Active Directory for new or unrecognized accounts, since many groups create accounts for persistence (Akira "itadm", Blackcat "aadmin", Medusa and Ghost domain accounts).
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Prioritize Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) on internet-facing systems: VPN appliances (Cisco ASA/FTD, Fortinet FortiOS), remote management (ConnectWise ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709), Microsoft Exchange (ProxyShell, ProxyNotShell), SharePoint, ColdFusion and Fortinet EMS. Use KEV, EPSS, CVSS and SSVC to prioritize. Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) appears in every advisory in this corpus.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Allowlist approved remote access tools and block unauthorized or portable RMM software (AnyDesk, Splashtop, ScreenConnect, Atera, SimpleHelp, Quick Assist), which nearly every group abuses (T1219). Restrict RDP to known users through a VPN or jump host with MFA, log attempts, enforce lockouts and close unused ports such as 3389, 445 and 21.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Segment networks into tiers so critical systems (EHR, virtualization, backups, domain controllers) are isolated. Apply least privilege and just-in-time administrative access, disable admin accounts when not needed, and require admin credentials to install software.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Deploy EDR on all hosts including virtual machines and monitor for lateral movement. Enable command-line auditing, process tracking and enhanced PowerShell logging with at least 180 days retention, forwarded to a hardened central log server. Alert on scanning, admin account changes, unexpected scripts and tampering with security tools (T1562.001). Restrict PowerShell and disable command-line and scripting activity where not required.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Train users to recognize phishing, helpdesk impersonation by phone, SMS or Microsoft Teams (Black Basta, Blackcat), fake browser updates and ClickFix fake CAPTCHAs (Interlock). Add external-sender email banners, disable hyperlinks in received email, use DNS filtering, and enforce DMARC, DKIM and SPF.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: Ransomware Prevention Baseline (cross-advisory synthesis)
text: Every advisory recommends exercising security controls against the listed MITRE ATT&CK techniques, comparing detection and prevention results, and tuning controls based on the outcome.
publisher: Group 3B synthesis of CISA #StopRansomware advisory mitigation sections

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1486: Data Encrypted for Impact
text:
T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact (tactics: impact; platforms: ESXi, IaaS, Linux, macOS, Windows).
Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. They can attempt to render stored data inaccessible by encrypting files or data on local and remote drives and withholding access to a decryption key. This may be done in order to extract monetary compensation from a victim in exchange for decryption or a decryption key (ransomware) or to render data permanently inaccessible in cases where the key is not saved or transmitted.

In the case of ransomware, it is typical that common user files like Office documents, PDFs, images, videos, audio, text, and source code files will be encrypted (and often renamed and/or tagged with specific file markers). Adversaries may need to first employ other behaviors, such as File and Directory Permissions Modification or System Shutdown/Reboot, in order to unlock and/or gain access to manipulate these files. In some cases, adversaries may encrypt critical system files, disk partitions, and the MBR. Adversaries may also encrypt virtual machines hosted on ESXi or other hypervisors. 

To maximize impact on the target organization, malware designed for encrypting data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging other attack techniques like Valid Accounts, OS Credential Dumping, and SMB/Windows Admin Shares. Encryption malware may also leverage Internal Defacement, such as changing victim wallpapers or ESXi server login mes

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1486: Data Encrypted for Impact
text:
Mitigations for T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact:
- M1040 Behavior Prevention on Endpoint: On Windows 10, enable cloud-delivered protection and Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules to block the execution of files that resemble ransomware. In AWS environments, create an IAM policy to restrict or block the use of SSE-C on S3 buckets.
- M1053 Data Backup: Consider implementing IT disaster recovery plans that contain procedures for regularly taking and testing data backups that can be used to restore organizational data. Ensure backups are stored off system and is protected from common methods adversaries may use to gain access and destroy the backups to prevent recovery. title: MITRE ATT&CK T1486: Data Encrypted for Impact
text:
Detection strategies for T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact:
- DET0215 Detection of Multi-Platform File Encryption for Impact
  - (Windows) High-frequency file write operations using uncommon extensions, followed by ransom note creation, registry tampering, or shadow copy deletion. Often uses CLI tools like vssadmin, wbadmin, cipher, or PowerShell. Log sources: WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=11); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=2)
  - (Linux) Encryption via custom or open-source tools (e.g., openssl, gpg, aescrypt) recursively targeting user or system directories. Also includes overwrite of existing data and ransom note drops. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (openat, write, rename, unlink); auditd:SYSCALL (execve)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490: Inhibit System Recovery
text:
T1490 Inhibit System Recovery (tactics: impact; platforms: Containers, ESXi, IaaS, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Windows).
Adversaries may delete or remove built-in data and turn off services designed to aid in the recovery of a corrupted system to prevent recovery. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may disable or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact. Furthermore, adversaries may disable recovery notifications, then corrupt backups.

A number of native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:

* `vssadmin.exe` can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system - `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet`
* Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies - `wmic shadowcopy delete`
* `wbadmin.exe` can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog - `wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet`
* `bcdedit.exe` can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data - `bcdedit.exe /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no`
* `REAgentC.exe` can be used to disable Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) repair/recovery options of an infected system
* `diskshadow.exe` can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system - `diskshadow delete shadows all`

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490: Inhibit System Recovery
text:
Mitigations for T1490 Inhibit System Recovery:
- M1038 Execution Prevention: Consider using application control configured to block execution of utilities such as `diskshadow.exe` that may not be required for a given system or network to prevent potential misuse by adversaries.
- M1028 Operating System Configuration: Consider technical controls to prevent the disabling of services or deletion of files involved in system recovery. Additionally, ensure that WinRE is enabled using the following command: `reagentc /enable`.
- M1018 User Account Management: Limit the user accounts that have access to backups to only those required. In AWS environments, consider using Service Control Policies to restrict API calls to delete backups, snapshots, and images.
- M1053 Data Backup: Consider implementing IT disaster recovery plans that contain procedures for taking regular data backups that can be used to restore organizational data. Ensure backups are stored off system and is protected from common methods adversaries may use to gain access and destroy the backups to prevent recovery. title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490: Inhibit System Recovery
text:
Detection strategies for T1490 Inhibit System Recovery:
- DET0329 Behavioral Detection for T1490 - Inhibit System Recovery
  - (Windows) Process chains that use native utilities (vssadmin, wbadmin, diskshadow, bcdedit, REAgentC, wmic) with arguments to delete shadow copies, disable recovery, or remove backup catalogs Log sources: WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1); WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Backup (Windows Backup Catalog deletion or catalog corruption); WinEventLog:System (Service stopped or RecoveryDisabled set via REAgentC); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=13, 14)
  - (Linux) Shell utilities or scripts deleting `/etc/systemd/system/rescue.target`, `/etc/fstab` backups, or `/boot/efi` partitions; chattr used to block snapshot auto-recovery Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (chattr, rm, shred, dd run on recovery directories or partitions); auditd:CONFIG_CHANGE (/etc/fstab, /etc/systemd/*)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1489: Service Stop
text:
T1489 Service Stop (tactics: impact; platforms: ESXi, IaaS, Linux, macOS, Windows).
Adversaries may stop or disable services on a system to render those services unavailable to legitimate users. Stopping critical services or processes can inhibit or stop response to an incident or aid in the adversary's overall objectives to cause damage to the environment. 

Adversaries may accomplish this by disabling individual services of high importance to an organization, such as `MSExchangeIS`, which will make Exchange content inaccessible. In some cases, adversaries may stop or disable many or all services to render systems unusable. Services or processes may not allow for modification of their data stores while running. Adversaries may stop services or processes in order to conduct Data Destruction or Data Encrypted for Impact on the data stores of services like Exchange and SQL Server, or on virtual machines hosted on ESXi infrastructure.

Threat actors may also disable or stop service in cloud environments. For example, by leveraging the `DisableAPIServiceAccess` API in AWS, a threat actor may prevent the service from creating service-linked roles on new accounts in the AWS Organization.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1489: Service Stop
text:
Mitigations for T1489 Service Stop:
- M1030 Network Segmentation: Operate intrusion detection, analysis, and response systems on a separate network from the production environment to lessen the chances that an adversary can see and interfere with critical response functions.
- M1018 User Account Management: Limit privileges of user accounts and groups so that only authorized administrators can interact with service changes and service configurations.
- M1060 Out-of-Band Communications Channel: Develop and enforce security policies that include the use of out-of-band communication channels for critical communications during a security incident.
- M1024 Restrict Registry Permissions: Ensure proper registry permissions are in place to inhibit adversaries from disabling or interfering with critical services.
- M1022 Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Ensure proper process and file permissions are in place to inhibit adversaries from disabling or interfering with critical services.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1489: Service Stop
text:
Detection strategies for T1489 Service Stop:
- DET0021 Behavioral Detection for Service Stop across Platforms
  - (Windows) Adversary disables or stops critical services (e.g., Exchange, SQL, AV, endpoint monitoring) using native utilities or API calls, often preceding destructive actions (T1485, T1486). Behavioral chain: Elevated execution context + stop-service or sc.exe or ChangeServiceConfigW + terminated or disabled service + possible follow-up file manipulation. Log sources: WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1); WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4672); WinEventLog:System (EventCode=7036); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=4)
  - (Linux) Adversary executes systemctl or service stop targeting high-value services (e.g., mysql, sshd), possibly followed by rm or shred against data stores. Behavioral chain: sudo/su usage + stop command + /var/log/messages or syslog entries + file access/delete. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (execve of systemctl or service stop); auditd:SYSCALL (unlink/unlinkat on service binaries or data targets); linux:syslog (service stopped messages)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1485: Data Destruction
text:
T1485 Data Destruction (tactics: impact; platforms: Containers, ESXi, IaaS, Linux, macOS, Windows).
Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources. Data destruction is likely to render stored data irrecoverable by forensic techniques through overwriting files or data on local and remote drives. Common operating system file deletion commands such as `del` and `rm` often only remove pointers to files without wiping the contents of the files themselves, making the files recoverable by proper forensic methodology. This behavior is distinct from Disk Content Wipe and Disk Structure Wipe because individual files are destroyed rather than sections of a storage disk or the disk's logical structure.

Adversaries may attempt to overwrite files and directories with randomly generated data to make it irrecoverable. In some cases politically oriented image files have been used to overwrite data.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware designed for destroying data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like Valid Accounts, OS Credential Dumping, and SMB/Windows Admin Shares..

In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage access to delete cloud storage objects, machine images, database instances, and other infrastructure crucial to operations to damage an organization or their customers. Similarly, they may delete virtual machines fr

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1485: Data Destruction
text:
Mitigations for T1485 Data Destruction:
- M1032 Multi-factor Authentication: Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete for cloud storage resources, such as AWS S3 buckets, to prevent unauthorized deletion of critical data and infrastructure. MFA delete requires additional authentication steps, making it significantly more difficult for adversaries to destroy data without proper credentials. This additional security layer helps protect against the impact of data de
- M1053 Data Backup: Consider implementing IT disaster recovery plans that contain procedures for taking regular data backups that can be used to restore organizational data. Ensure backups are stored off system and protected from common methods adversaries may use to gain access and destroy the backups to prevent recovery.
- M1018 User Account Management: In cloud environments, limit permissions to modify cloud bucket lifecycle policies (e.g., `PutLifecycleConfiguration` in AWS) to only those accounts that require it. In AWS environments, consider using Service Control policies to limit the use of the `PutBucketLifecycle` API call.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1485: Data Destruction
text:
Detection strategies for T1485 Data Destruction:
- DET0146 Detection of Data Destruction Across Platforms via Mass Overwrite and Deletion Patterns
  - (Windows) Adversary spawns command-line tools (e.g., del, cipher /w, SDelete) or scripts to recursively delete or overwrite user/system files. This may be correlated with abnormal file IO activity, registry writes, or tampering in critical system directories. Log sources: WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=11); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=23)
  - (Linux) Massive recursive deletions or overwrites via `rm -rf`, `shred`, `dd`, or wiper binaries. May include unlink syscalls, deletion of known config/data paths, or sequential overwrite patterns. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (unlink, unlinkat, openat, write); auditd:SYSCALL (execve)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1529: System Shutdown/Reboot
text:
T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot (tactics: impact; platforms: ESXi, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Windows).
Adversaries may shutdown/reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems. Operating systems may contain commands to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a machine or network device. In some cases, these commands may also be used to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a remote computer or network device via Network Device CLI (e.g. `reload`). They may also include shutdown/reboot of a virtual machine via hypervisor / cloud consoles or command line tools.

Shutting down or rebooting systems may disrupt access to computer resources for legitimate users while also impeding incident response/recovery.

Adversaries may also use Windows API functions, such as `InitializeSystemShutdownExW` or `ExitWindowsEx`, to force a system to shut down or reboot. Alternatively, the `NtRaiseHardError`or `ZwRaiseHardError` Windows API functions with the `ResponseOption` parameter set to `OptionShutdownSystem` may deliver a “blue screen of death” (BSOD) to a system. In order to leverage these API functions, an adversary may need to acquire `SeShutdownPrivilege` (e.g., via Access Token Manipulation).
 In some cases, the system may not be able to boot again. 

Adversaries may attempt to shutdown/reboot a system after impacting it in other ways, such as Disk Structure Wipe or Inhibit System Recovery, to hasten the intended effects on system availability.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1529: System Shutdown/Reboot
text:
Detection strategies for T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot:
- DET0559 Multi-Platform Shutdown or Reboot Detection via Execution and Host Status Events
  - (Windows) Correlate process execution of shutdown/reboot commands (e.g., shutdown.exe, restart-computer) with host status change logs (Event IDs 1074, 6006) and absence of related administrative context (e.g., user not in Helpdesk group). Log sources: WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=1074); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1)
  - (Linux) Detect 'shutdown', 'reboot', or 'systemctl poweroff' executions with auditd/syslog and absence of scheduled maintenance windows or approved user context. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (execve=/sbin/shutdown or /sbin/reboot); linux:syslog (system is powering down)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1657: Financial Theft
text:
T1657 Financial Theft (tactics: impact; platforms: Linux, macOS, Office Suite, SaaS, Windows).
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware, business email compromise (BEC) and fraud, "pig butchering," bank hacking, and exploiting cryptocurrency networks. 

Adversaries may Compromise Accounts to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds. In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize Impersonation of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary. This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after Data Encrypted for Impact and Exfiltration of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary. Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as Data Destruction and business

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1657: Financial Theft
text:
Mitigations for T1657 Financial Theft:
- M1017 User Training: Train and encourage users to identify social engineering techniques used to enable financial theft. Also consider training users on procedures to prevent and respond to swatting and doxing, acts increasingly deployed by financially motivated groups to further coerce victims into satisfying ransom/extortion demands.
- M1018 User Account Management: Limit access/authority to execute sensitive transactions, and switch to systems and procedures designed to authenticate/approve payments and purchase requests outside of insecure communication lines such as email.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1657: Financial Theft
text:
Detection strategies for T1657 Financial Theft:
- DET0495 Detection Strategy for Financial Theft
  - (Windows) Monitor for anomalous access to financial applications, browser-based banking sessions, or enterprise ERP systems from Windows endpoints. Detect mass emailing of payment instructions, sudden rule changes in Outlook for financial staff, or use of clipboard data exfiltration tied to cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4624, 4648); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1)
  - (Linux) Monitor server and endpoint logs for unusual outbound network connections to cryptocurrency nodes, unauthorized scripts accessing financial systems, or automation targeting payment file formats. Detect curl/wget activity aimed at exfiltrating transaction data or credentials from financial apps. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (execve: Execution of curl, wget, or custom scripts accessing financial endpoints); linux:syslog (Authentication attempts into finance-related servers from unusual IPs or times)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1566: Phishing
text:
T1566 Phishing (tactics: initial-access; platforms: Identity Provider, Linux, macOS, Office Suite, SaaS, Windows).
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services (like social media platforms) or delivered via calendar invites. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., Email Hiding Rules). Another way to accomplish this is by Email Spoofing the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools, or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware, or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., User Execution).

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1566: Phishing
text:
Mitigations for T1566 Phishing:
- M1047 Audit: Perform audits or scans of systems, permissions, insecure software, insecure configurations, etc. to identify potential weaknesses.
- M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention: Network intrusion prevention systems and systems designed to scan and remove malicious email attachments or links can be used to block activity.
- M1054 Software Configuration: Use anti-spoofing and email authentication mechanisms to filter messages based on validity checks of the sender domain (using SPF) and integrity of messages (using DKIM). Enabling these mechanisms within an organization (through policies such as DMARC) may enable recipients (intra-org and cross domain) to perform similar message filtering and validation.
- M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content: Determine if certain websites or attachment types (ex: .scr, .exe, .pif, .cpl, etc.) that can be used for phishing are necessary for business operations and consider blocking access if activity cannot be monitored well or if it poses a significant risk.
- M1049 Antivirus/Antimalware: Anti-virus can automatically quarantine suspicious files.
- M1017 User Training: Users can be trained to identify social engineering techniques and phishing emails.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1566: Phishing
text:
Detection strategies for T1566 Phishing:
- DET0070 Detection Strategy for Phishing across platforms.
  - (Windows) Unusual inbound email activity where attachments or embedded URLs are delivered to users followed by execution of new processes or suspicious document behavior. Detection involves correlating email metadata, file creation, and network activity after a phishing message is received. Log sources: m365:unified (Send/Receive: Emails with suspicious sender domains, spoofed headers, or anomalous attachment types); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=11); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1)
  - (Linux) Monitor for malicious payload delivery through phishing where attachments or URLs in email clients (e.g., Thunderbird, mutt) result in unusual file creation or outbound network connections. Focus on correlation between mail logs, file writes, and execution activity. Log sources: Application:Mail (Inbound messages with anomalous headers, spoofed SPF/DKIM failures); auditd:SYSCALL (execve: Execution of scripts or binaries sourced from mail directories (/var/mail, ~/Maildir))

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application
text:
T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application (tactics: initial-access; platforms: Containers, ESXi, IaaS, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Windows).
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets. On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers. Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve Exploitation for Stealth or Exploitation for Client Execution.

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the Cloud Instance Metadata API), exploit container host access via Escape to Host, or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application
text:
Mitigations for T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application:
- M1048 Application Isolation and Sandboxing: Application isolation will limit what other processes and system features the exploited target can access.
- M1037 Filter Network Traffic: Restrict outbound network traffic from public-facing servers to prevent unauthorized connections from initiating communications with attacker-controlled infrastructure. While this may not prevent the initial exploitation, it limits the attacker's ability to verify and control the compromised server post-exploit, reducing the overall impact of the attack.
- M1030 Network Segmentation: Segment externally facing servers and services from the rest of the network with a DMZ or on separate hosting infrastructure.
- M1016 Vulnerability Scanning: Regularly scan externally facing systems for vulnerabilities and establish procedures to rapidly patch systems when critical vulnerabilities are discovered through scanning and through public disclosure.
- M1026 Privileged Account Management: Use least privilege for service accounts will limit what permissions the exploited process gets on the rest of the system.
- M1050 Exploit Protection: Web Application Firewalls may be used to limit exposure of applications to prevent exploit traffic from reaching the application.
- M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network: Ensure that all publicly exposed services are actually intended to be so, and restrict access to any that should only be available internally.
- M1051 Update Software: Update software regularly by employing patch management for externally exposed applications.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application
text:
Detection strategies for T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application:
- DET0080 Exploit Public-Facing Application – multi-signal correlation (request → error → post-exploit process/egress)
  - (Windows) Adversary sends crafted HTTP/S (or other service) input to an Internet-facing app (IIS/ASP.NET, API, device portal). Chain: (1) abnormal request patterns to public endpoint → (2) elevated 4xx/5xx or unusual methods/paths → (3) server process (w3wp.exe/other service) spawns shell/LOLbins or loads non-standard modules → (4) optional outbound callback from the host/container. Log sources: ApplicationLog:IIS (IIS W3C logs in C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC* (spikes in 5xx, RCE/SQLi/path traversal/JNDI patterns)); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=7); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=3, 22)
  - (Linux) Adversary exploits Apache/Nginx/app servers. Chain: (1) suspicious requests in access logs → (2) spike of 5xx or WAF blocks → (3) web server or interpreter (apache2/nginx/php-fpm/node/python) spawns /bin/sh, curl, wget, socat, or writes webshell → (4) outbound callback. Log sources: ApplicationLog:WebServer (/var/log/httpd/access_log, /var/log/apache2/access.log, /var/log/nginx/access.log with exploit indicators and burst errors); auditd:SYSCALL (execve); NSM:Flow (HTTP payloads with SQLi/LFI/JNDI/deserialization indicators)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1133: External Remote Services
text:
T1133 External Remote Services (tactics: persistence, initial-access; platforms: Containers, Linux, macOS, Windows).
Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services to initially access and/or persist within a network. Remote services such as VPNs, Citrix, and other access mechanisms allow users to connect to internal enterprise network resources from external locations. There are often remote service gateways that manage connections and credential authentication for these services. Services such as Windows Remote Management and VNC can also be used externally.

Access to Valid Accounts to use the service is often a requirement, which could be obtained through credential pharming or by obtaining the credentials from users after compromising the enterprise network. Access to remote services may be used as a redundant or persistent access mechanism during an operation.

Access may also be gained through an exposed service that doesn’t require authentication. In containerized environments, this may include an exposed Docker API, Kubernetes API server, kubelet, or web application such as the Kubernetes dashboard.

Adversaries may also establish persistence on network by configuring a Tor hidden service on a compromised system. Adversaries may utilize the tool `ShadowLink` to facilitate the installation and configuration of the Tor hidden service. Tor hidden service is then accessible via the Tor network because `ShadowLink` sets up a .onion address on the compromised system. `ShadowLink` may be used to forward any inbound connections to RDP, allowing the adversaries to have remote acces

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1133: External Remote Services
text:
Mitigations for T1133 External Remote Services:
- M1021 Restrict Web-Based Content: Restrict all traffic to and from public Tor nodes.
- M1030 Network Segmentation: Deny direct remote access to internal systems through the use of network proxies, gateways, and firewalls.
- M1042 Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Disable or block remotely available services that may be unnecessary.
- M1035 Limit Access to Resource Over Network: Limit access to remote services through centrally managed concentrators such as VPNs and other managed remote access systems.
- M1032 Multi-factor Authentication: Use strong two-factor or multi-factor authentication for remote service accounts to mitigate an adversary's ability to leverage stolen credentials, but be aware of Multi-Factor Authentication Interception techniques for some two-factor authentication implementations.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1133: External Remote Services
text:
Detection strategies for T1133 External Remote Services:
- DET0354 Behavior-chain detection for T1133 External Remote Services across Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers
  - (Windows) Unusual or unauthorized external remote access attempts (e.g., RDP, VPN, Citrix) → repeated failed logins followed by a successful session from uncommon geolocations or outside business hours → subsequent internal lateral movement or data exfiltration activities. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4776, 4625); WinEventLog:Application (VPN, Citrix, or remote access gateway logs showing external IP addresses); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=3, 22)
  - (Linux) Repeated SSH, VPN, or RDP gateway authentication attempts from external IPs → subsequent successful logon → remote shell or lateral movement activity (e.g., scp/sftp). Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (ssh logins or execve of remote commands); NSM:Connections (Failed password or accepted password for SSH users); NSM:Flow (connection: Inbound connections to SSH or VPN ports)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1078: Valid Accounts
text:
T1078 Valid Accounts (tactics: stealth, persistence, privilege-escalation, initial-access; platforms: Containers, ESXi, IaaS, Identity Provider, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Office Suite, SaaS, Windows).
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials may be used to bypass access controls placed on various resources on systems within the network and may even be used for persistent access to remote systems and externally available services, such as VPNs, Outlook Web Access, network devices, and remote desktop. Compromised credentials may also grant an adversary increased privilege to specific systems or access to restricted areas of the network. Adversaries may choose not to use malware or tools in conjunction with the legitimate access those credentials provide to make it harder to detect their presence.

In some cases, adversaries may abuse inactive accounts: for example, those belonging to individuals who are no longer part of an organization. Using these accounts may allow the adversary to evade detection, as the original account user will not be present to identify any anomalous activity taking place on their account.

The overlap of permissions for local, domain, and cloud accounts across a network of systems is of concern because the adversary may be able to pivot across accounts and systems to reach a high level of access (i.e., domain or enterprise administrator) to bypass access controls set within the enterprise.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1078: Valid Accounts
text:
Mitigations for T1078 Valid Accounts:
- M1027 Password Policies: Applications and appliances that utilize default username and password should be changed immediately after the installation, and before deployment to a production environment. When possible, applications that use SSH keys should be updated periodically and properly secured.

Policies should minimize (if not eliminate) reuse of passwords between different user accounts, especially employees using t
- M1018 User Account Management: Regularly audit user accounts for activity and deactivate or remove any that are no longer needed.
- M1026 Privileged Account Management: Audit domain and local accounts as well as their permission levels routinely to look for situations that could allow an adversary to gain wide access by obtaining credentials of a privileged account. These audits should also include if default accounts have been enabled, or if new local accounts are created that have not been authorized. Follow best practices for design and administration of an en
- M1032 Multi-factor Authentication: Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) across all account types, including default, local, domain, and cloud accounts, to prevent unauthorized access, even if credentials are compromised. MFA provides a critical layer of security by requiring multiple forms of verification beyond just a password. This measure significantly reduces the risk of adversaries abusing valid accounts to gain initial
- M1013 Application Developer Guidance: Ensure that applications do not store sensitive data or credentials insecurely. (e.g. plaintext credentials in code, published credentials in repositories, or credentials in public cloud storage).
- M1017 User Training: Applications may send push notifications to verify a login as a form of multi-factor authentication (MFA). Train users to only accept valid push notifications and to report suspicious push notifications.
- M1015 Active Directory Configuration: Disable legacy authentication, which does not support MFA, and require the use of modern authentication protocols instead.
- M1036 Account Use Policies: Use conditional access policies to block logins from non-compliant devices or from outside defined organization IP ranges.

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1078: Valid Accounts
text:
Detection strategies for T1078 Valid Accounts:
- DET0560 Detection of Valid Account Abuse Across Platforms
  - (Windows) Detection of compromised or misused valid accounts via anomalous logon patterns, abnormal logon types, and inconsistent geographic or time-based activity across Windows endpoints. Log sources: WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4624); WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4776, 4625); WinEventLog:Sysmon (EventCode=1)
  - (Linux) Detection of valid account misuse through SSH logins, sudo/su abuse, and service account anomalies outside expected patterns. Log sources: auditd:SYSCALL (execve); NSM:Connections (sshd or PAM logins)

title: MITRE ATT&CK T1189: Drive-by Compromise
text:
T1189 Drive-by Compromise (tactics: initial-access; platforms: Identity Provider, Linux, macOS, Windows).
Adversaries may gain access to a system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing. Multiple ways of delivering exploit code to a browser exist (i.e., Drive-by Target), including:
